newsitem.title: USA: Dole plays down expectations ahead of debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole plays down expectations ahead of debate.

text.p: First Bob Dole said, "If I show up, I will win." But now the Republican candidate is lowering expectations for his first debate on Sunday night with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Lowering expectations is part of a time-honored political game as candidates head for a face-off, and Dole is a keen player. He is spending Friday and Saturday rehearsing in his Florida condominium for the debate in Hartford, Connecticut, that will draw a huge television audience -- perhaps more than 90 million people.

Before walking into the Sea View apartment complex on Thursday night and slamming a door on the outside world, Dole spent the day making self-deprecating jokes about the encounter he and his aides hope will pump new life into his floundering campaign.

At one campaign event in Johnson City, Tennessee, Dole told reporters he didn't know how he would fare against Clinton, but added in a typical acerbic aside, "If I can find Hartford, I'll do alright."
Later, in front of campaign crowds, he joked about whether he would even show up and added, "This is the biggest audience I'll ever address, at least for the first few minutes."

Not to be outdone, Clinton is playing the same low expectations game as he preps for the debate at a resort in upstate New York. On Wednesday, his spokesman Mike McCurry described the president as "apprehensive" about the debate, saying Clinton felt his preparation was behind schedule after two days of intensive Middle East diplomacy this week.
This same week saw Dole all but drop out of the public eye as the 73-year-old candidate drastically cut back on appearances so he could prepare for the 90-minute debate.

He spent four days at his condo last week preparing, studying videotapes of Clinton's successful debates against George Bush in the 1992 campaign and memorizing a briefing book on the president's positions and -- most importantly for Dole -- Clinton's flip-flops on those positions.

Aides, meanwhile, worked up one-liners for possible use, and Tennessee Republican Senator Fred Thompson has been playing Clinton in a series of mock debates. Thompson is a former actor who specialized in bad-guy roles.

Some Dole critics charge that his preparations have wiped him off the public's radar screen. Both inside the party and out, there has been consternation over the generally slow pace of the campaign and at Dole's failure to make inroads against Clinton, as seen in most polls.
Dole seems well aware that time is running out for him to make an impact.

"One of our surveys showed that only 27 percent of the American people are tuned into the presidential race and that there are a lot of people out there who have yet to take note of what's happening," he said, adding that the debate was "great opportunity" to turn things around.
Dole and his handlers publicly stress that they are up against a masterful speaker in Clinton, while privately they pray their man can establish himself in 90 minutes as a viable alternative.

"Clinton's had 300 percent more experience debating in these circumstances," said Nelson Warfield, Dole's campaign spokesman, referring to Clinton's three debates with George Bush in the 1992 campaign.
Asked about the slow pace of the campaign, Warfield said, "You can't get out in front of the voters, until they get interested. You can't put your best stuff out until the stands are full of fans."
Meanwhile, Thompson, his pre-debate sparring partner, said, "Everybody knows how good Clinton is on his feet, but I think Senator Dole's honesty, knowledge and integrity will show through."
